title: PHP2Shell is a wake-up call for Filipino web developers

blocks.text: I am a PHP developer myself. For years, I have heard the familiar joke that “PHP is dead.” Yet the language continues to power websites, online stores, and business applications that people depend on daily.

For many Filipino developers, PHP has been a practical entry point into building software. Its accessibility and widespread hosting support have helped businesses establish their presence online. Across the local development community, it remains part of the infrastructure we build and maintain.
That is why PHP2Shell deserves our immediate attention.

The two critical vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, can allow an unauthenticated attacker, under certain conditions, to execute code on servers running PHP. The PHP Foundation has urged users to update immediately.

For a business owner, the implication is straightforward: an attacker could potentially run malicious code on the server supporting your website. Depending on the server’s permissions and connections, that could put customer information, business records, credentials, and other systems at risk.
This is a serious concern for Philippine businesses that rely on their websites for transactions, customer service, and everyday operations.

A functioning website does not prove that it is secure. Customers may still be able to place orders, employees may still be able to access their accounts, and the homepage may look perfectly normal. None of those observations confirms that the underlying software has been patched.
“We have not noticed anything unusual” is an insufficient response to a critical security advisory.

The long-running “PHP is dead” joke suddenly feels uncomfortable when the systems built with it face a threat capable of disrupting operations or compromising data. But declaring the language finished accomplishes little. What matters now is how quickly those responsible for affected systems respond.
The update cannot wait

PHP has released security fixes in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Its official announcement states that there are no complete mitigations and urges users to update immediately. Administrators should follow the official instructions or their operating system provider’s guidance for patched packages.
Developers and system administrators should identify affected installations, prioritize exposed services, apply the appropriate updates, and verify that the patched software is running.
Updating a website’s content management system or plugins should not be mistaken for updating PHP itself. Website owners need confirmation that the underlying runtime has been addressed.
Businesses using managed hosting should contact their providers and ask specific questions: Is our installation affected? Has the security patch been applied? Has its deployment been verified?
Those questions deserve clear answers.

Developers and agencies should also proactively contact clients whose systems they maintain. Many business owners will never encounter a PHP security advisory, much less understand its implications. They depend on technical professionals to translate that warning into action.
Waiting for the client to ask shifts the burden to someone who may have no way of recognizing the danger.
Maintenance is a business responsibility
PHP2Shell also exposes a familiar weakness in how organizations treat technology.

Businesses will allocate money for a new website, approve its design, and celebrate its launch. Maintenance can become an afterthought, with no clear budget or person responsible for keeping the system secure.

That arrangement leaves an obvious gap. When a critical vulnerability emerges, who checks whether the business is affected? Who can access the server? Who authorizes and applies the update? Who confirms that it worked?
Those responsibilities should already be assigned before an emergency happens.
A website remains an operational responsibility for as long as people use it. Its maintenance requirements continue after the developer hands it over and after the final invoice is paid.

Smaller businesses may have limited resources, but they still need a clear maintenance arrangement. Even a basic agreement identifying who monitors security advisories and handles urgent updates is better than discovering during an incident that everyone assumed someone else was responsible.

As a PHP developer, I recognize what this language has made possible. It has helped developers build careers and businesses deliver useful services. That contribution makes responding responsibly to this threat even more necessary.
We should take the warning seriously, communicate clearly with those affected, and apply the available fixes promptly.
If you learn that your system is affected, act immediately. The time to update is before your customers and your business experience the consequences.
